A timed-out join leaves remaining flusher workers alive

For multiple workers, once the shared join deadline is exhausted this `break` exits the loop before terminating the current or any later worker. `next_step.join(timeout)` may consume the entire timeout before the loop begins, and waiting for the first flusher can consume it for all subsequent workers. A worker blocked in Kafka `future.result()` will not observe the cooperative stopped flag, so those unvisited workers remain running after consumer shutdown/rebalance and can continue operating on revoked shards. Terminate all still-alive process workers after the deadline rather than breaking out before cleanup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

false_positives.candidate:
The new flusher process count accepts values that break or defeat the limit

`--flusher-processes` accepts zero and negative values. A negative value reaches `SpanFlusher`, makes `num_processes` negative, creates no process-map entries, and then raises `KeyError` while assigning the first shard. Zero is treated as false by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, unexpectedly starting one worker per shard rather than rejecting the invalid limit. Restrict this option to integers of at least one and validate direct constructor callers as well.

The new limit test never exercises the multiprocessing implementation

Passing `produce_to_pipe=messages.append` selects the `threading.Thread` branch in `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shards`, so this test only checks the in-memory shard map and starts no spawned worker. The production path added by this change initializes Sentry, pickles a shard-specific buffer, creates `SpawnProcess` workers, and must handle their lifecycle; none of that is covered. Add a test that runs the process branch (with Kafka production mocked or an interprocess-safe sink) and verifies shard flushing and shutdown/restart behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing one assignment permanently disables the factory-owned pool

The pool is created once on `ResultsStrategyFactory` and is shared by every strategy returned from `create_with_partitions`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` shuts that shared pool down. After a Kafka partition revoke/reassignment causes Arroyo to close/terminate one strategy and create another from the same factory, the new strategy receives the already-shut-down pool and no workers. On Python 3.13, `Queue.put()` then raises `ShutDown`, and `submit()` catches that error and marks the offset complete, so the new strategy can commit messages that were never processed. On older Python versions, the puts succeed into queues with no workers and offsets never advance. The pool must be scoped to a single strategy assignment or recreated/reset after strategy teardown.

The purported graceful shutdown abandons queued work before a final commit

Workers are marked `shutdown=True` before their queues are shut down. A worker that is currently processing exits after that item, and a worker that was blocked in `get()` processes at most one item before its next loop-condition check exits; remaining queued items are never drained. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` also stops and joins the commit thread before this worker shutdown, so an item finishing during shutdown has no later commit opportunity. This causes arbitrary accepted work to be replayed after normal deploys/rebalances, potentially duplicating side effects and creating large restart backlogs. Shutdown should drain accepted work (or deliberately cancel it with a coordinated retry policy) and commit completed offsets after the drain.

The worker queues are unbounded, so the new mode provides no backpressure

`queue.Queue()` defaults to `maxsize=0`, meaning `FixedQueuePool.submit()` never blocks regardless of how far a slow worker falls behind. The consumer will continue decoding and retaining every fetched message (including both the decoded result and original `Message`) in memory while lag grows. A slow remote-subscription handler can therefore cause unbounded memory growth and OOM the consumer, contrary to the strategy's stated backpressure guarantee. Configure a bounded queue size and integrate blocking/full-queue handling with the consumer's polling/backpressure behavior.

Use of Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs breaks supported runtimes

`queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged here), leaving workers blocked forever in `get()`. Each subsequent `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` then waits the full timeout, so the default 20 queues can make every consumer shutdown take roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon workers. An exception raised while processing work also attempts to resolve `queue.ShutDown` in the exception handler and can terminate the worker with an `AttributeError`. Use a compatible sentinel/event-based shutdown mechanism or require and enforce Python 3.13.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Explicit-denial-cache test does not prove the denial cache is consulted

The test comment says the normal permission cache should allow access if checked, but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. Without the new denial-cache lookup, `Check` would still return denied from that false value (and then from the empty fake store), so the test passes even if the denial cache is removed or bypassed. Store `true` for the dashboard scope and assert that no permission-store lookup occurs, so the test verifies denial-cache precedence.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key encoding is ambiguous for valid resource UIDs

`name` and `parent` are concatenated with `_` without escaping or length-prefixing. For example, a denial for name `a_b` with parent `c` produces the same key as a check for name `a` with parent `b_c`. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly short-circuit an allowed check for another resource for 30 seconds. Use an unambiguous structured encoding or a hash of separately serialized fields.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache conflates anonymous and renderer identities

The denial key contains only `UserUID`, not `IdentityType`. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` therefore use the same key for a namespace/action/resource/folder. If an anonymous request is denied for a private dashboard, line 154 stores that denial; a subsequent renderer check for the same dashboard exits at line 117 as denied even though `getRendererPermissions` would grant dashboard reads. This permits cross-identity cache poisoning and can be used to keep renderer access denied by repeatedly causing anonymous checks. Include the identity type (or the full subject) in the denial-cache key.

Per-resource denial entries allow unbounded cache cardinality

Every denied check writes a distinct cache entry derived from the caller-supplied resource name and folder. A caller can issue checks for continuously changing nonexistent resource IDs, causing both the database fallback and one new denial-cache entry per request. The in-process service uses a local cache without a capacity limit at construction, and expired entries may remain until its cleanup interval, so this turns arbitrary request cardinality into cache memory growth. Use a size-bounded/admission-controlled cache or avoid caching arbitrary negative resource lookups.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence action is a no-op for Grafana-only list rows

The new GrafanaRuleListItem supplies only promRule, so rule is undefined. The menu can still expose “Silence notifications” using the new Grafana Prometheus ability, and its handler sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but this render condition only accepts a Grafana ruler rule. Clicking the visible menu item therefore produces no drawer or feedback in the new alert list. Render a Prometheus-compatible silence drawer (or do not expose the action until one is available).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete is hidden for every Grafana-only list row

The new list passes rulerRule as undefined, but this condition requires a ruler rule before rendering Delete. As a result, even users with a permitted Grafana Prometheus delete ability cannot delete a Grafana-managed rule from the list. In this caller, handleDelete ignores the ruler-rule argument and already has the identifier needed for useDeleteModal, so the stale rulerRule guard removes a previously supported operation.

Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable by combined-rule abilities

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from rule.group. It now delegates after discarding the CombinedRule and useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated to false. Any existing caller of useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities with a federated datasource rule will therefore consider update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent-delete supported when permissions otherwise allow them, instead of preserving the former federated-rule protection.

Grafana recording rules lost the export action

ModifyExport is now supported only when isAlertingRule is true. GrafanaPromRuleDTO also represents Grafana-managed recording rules, and the previous ruler-based implementation used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which covered both alerting and recording rules. Because the new list has no ruler fallback, recording rules with export permission no longer show Export even though the existing list supported exporting them.

Grafana rule view links no longer preserve the originating list route

The replaced GrafanaRuleLoader constructed the view URL with createReturnTo(), while the replacement omits returnTo entirely. Opening a rule from a filtered or hierarchical alert list now loses the list URL and filter state used by the rule view's in-page return navigation, sending users back to the default location rather than their originating list.

GrafanaGroupLoader documentation still claims it loads Ruler data

The component now issues only useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery and no longer reads the Ruler endpoint, but its documentation says it loads from both Prometheus and Ruler endpoints. The nearby expectedRulesCount comment also describes a Ruler response. This is misleading for future maintainers investigating the component's consistency and request behavior.

Pause and unpause are unavailable after removing the ruler rule

GrafanaRuleListItem intentionally calls this menu without rulerRule, while canPause is now allowed to be calculated from promRule. This condition still additionally requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule), so it is always false for the new Grafana list and users cannot pause or resume rules there despite having the displayed Prometheus-side ability. The menu needs a Prometheus-backed pause implementation or a compatible rule input.

Ruler fallback can re-enable duplication of plugin-provided rules

For a Grafana-only list row, rulerRule is undefined. useAllRulerRuleAbilities consequently treats it as neither provisioned nor plugin-provided, so when the ruler is available and the user has create permission its duplicate ability can be allowed. This OR expression then overrides the Grafana Prometheus ability, which correctly rejects plugin-provided rules based on their labels. Plugin-provided Grafana rules can therefore regain the Duplicate action merely because the obsolete ruler-side check has no rule to inspect.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Sharded queries now apply template processing once per shard batch after already processing it

This expands each target before shard discovery, but the resulting targets are later put into subRequest while retaining request.scopedVars and request.filters. runSplitQuery then calls applyTemplateVariables again for every shard group at querySplitting.ts:299. Template replacement is not generally idempotent: a literal value produced by the first expansion that contains a variable token can be expanded on the second pass, and ad-hoc filter rewriting is also rerun on the already rewritten selector. Consequently the final query can depend on how many shard groups were created. Preserve the initially interpolated targets for the inner splitter without reapplying templates, or explicitly mark/clear the already-consumed interpolation inputs.

Targets that interpolate to an empty expression are still executed

The expression-presence filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A target such as an optional query variable whose value resolves to an empty string therefore remains in the split groups and is passed to Loki with an empty expr, which can make an otherwise valid grouped request fail. The same pre-interpolation filtering order was added to shardQuerySplitting.ts:50; both entry points should filter out empty expressions after interpolation (while still skipping hidden targets before it).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Completed plugin-request logs no longer include the trace ID

The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as `traceID` to every `Plugin Request Completed` entry. That extraction was removed. The new contextual middleware only installs endpoint, plugin, datasource, and user attributes, so materializing the logger with `FromContext` does not supply the removed trace field. This breaks correlation between backend plugin request logs and distributed traces; retain the explicit trace attribute or add it when building the contextual attributes, and cover it with a logging test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger drops log observations when LoggerMiddleware calls FromContext

`LoggerMiddleware` now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`, but this fake returns a newly allocated, unreferenced `TestLogger`. Tests that inject a `TestLogger` and inspect the original instance will observe zero log calls, and cannot verify the completed-request log or its attributes. Make `FromContext` return the same fake or a contextual clone sharing the same recorded log storage, then add coverage for the migrated contextual logging behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding a required method to the exported Logger interface is source-incompatible

`Logger` is an exported interface, and adding `FromContext` means every existing implementation, wrapper, fake, or downstream mock of `pkg/plugins/log.Logger` will no longer compile until it implements the new method. This is a breaking API change beyond the middleware rename. Preserve compatibility by keeping `Logger` unchanged and introducing a separate optional contextual-logger interface that callers can type-assert, or explicitly version/document this breaking contract change.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The count-then-insert limit check is not atomic

The active-device count is queried in one database session and the later upsert is performed in another, with no transaction or locking between them. Concurrent requests with different device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and each insert successfully, permanently exceeding the configured limit for the 30-day window. The per-process local cache does not prevent this across simultaneous requests or Grafana instances. Admission needs an atomic/serialized database operation, and a concurrent test should cover the limit boundary.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A rejected device is cached and bypasses the limit on retry

`tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` determines whether it may be admitted. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first authentication fails, but the cache entry remains. A retry with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` on that server returns early at line 83 without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` grants anonymous access for roughly the cache TTL. Move cache insertion until after a successful store operation, or remove the entry on every store error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
The new anonymous device-limit setting is undocumented

`auth.anonymous.device_limit` is parsed here, but no defaults/configuration documentation file is updated in this PR. Administrators therefore have no discoverable configuration key or explanation that zero disables the limit and that the cap applies to devices active in the last 30 days.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every selected ID

This log statement is reached only after `fetchIDs` succeeded, so `err` is nil, yet it emits an Error log containing the complete ID slice. The same pattern occurs for the post-delete, max-count, and orphan-tag paths. Normal cleanup therefore produces error-level events and serializes up to an entire configured batch of IDs twice per batch, causing misleading alerting and potentially very large log ingestion during a backlog. Use an appropriate non-error level and log counts rather than full ID lists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The change increases the cadence of every cleanup job by tenfold

Changing the shared cleanup ticker from ten minutes to one minute does not only retry annotation cleanup; it also runs snapshot deletion, dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, invite expiration, short-URL cleanup, and query-history row-limit enforcement ten times as often. If a run lasts longer than a minute, the ticker also leaves a pending tick, allowing another full run to start immediately after it finishes. This substantially increases background database work for unrelated services; retain the existing global cadence and schedule any needed annotation retry separately.

false_positives.candidate:
Configured batch sizes can exceed database bind-parameter limits

The non-SQLite path creates one bind placeholder for every fetched ID, with no chunking or limit enforcement. A configured cleanup batch above 65,535 IDs causes MySQL/PostgreSQL prepared statements to fail due to their parameter-count limits; the same cleanup then retries and fails every cycle. The previous subquery-based delete did not consume one bind parameter per row. Split deletes into backend-safe chunks or validate the configuration against the supported limit.

SQLite large-batch SQL construction is quadratic

For SQLite batches over 999, each loop iteration formats a new string containing the entire accumulated ID list. This repeatedly copies the growing list, making construction O(n²) in both allocation and copy work. The newly added test configures a 32,767-item batch, and production batches of that size can spend substantial time and memory in this loop before issuing the delete. Build the list with a strings.Builder/byte buffer or delete in bounded chunks.

The new test uses a Go 1.21 builtin while the repository targets Go 1.20

`min` is a predeclared builtin only starting with Go 1.21. This repository's Go 1.20 language version cannot compile either this use or the equivalent use on line 286, so `go test` fails before the cleanup tests run. Replace these with a local helper or explicit end-index calculation compatible with the supported toolchain.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful delete metrics use an object name as the resource label

The third argument to recordStorageDuration is the resource/kind label; every other mode-3 path passes options.Kind. This successful-delete path passes name instead, creating a distinct Prometheus time series for every deleted object and making success and failure metrics use incompatible labels. A workload deleting many unique names can cause avoidable metric-cardinality growth. Pass options.Kind here.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several mode-3 duration measurements are recorded against the wrong store

When Storage.Create fails, this records a legacy duration rather than a storage duration; Update has the same error at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 records a storage duration. This hides primary failures and reports legacy failures as storage failures, so dashboards and alerts cannot accurately detect replication or unified-storage health. Record each operation on its corresponding collector.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
A primary NotFound no longer cleans up a stale legacy object

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error. The prior implementation treated a unified-storage NotFound specially: it still issued Legacy.Delete while returning the primary NotFound result. If the stores have already drifted, deleting an object that is absent in unified storage now leaves the stale legacy object intact and still available through legacy paths (or after rollback). Retain the legacy cleanup attempt for primary NotFound errors.

Asynchronous replica writes can be applied out of order

Each successful primary write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a unified Create followed by a unified Delete can schedule a slow legacy Create and a fast legacy Delete; the delete runs first against an absent legacy object, then the delayed create leaves the object present in legacy after it is deleted in unified storage. Since mode 3 reads unified storage, this divergence is hidden until a legacy endpoint is used or a rollback occurs. Replica writes need a serialized queue or per-key ordering mechanism.

Every write creates an unbounded 10-second background operation

There is no queue, semaphore, or worker limit around the goroutine per write. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, each incoming write can retain a goroutine, request data, and a legacy connection attempt for up to ten seconds. At normal write volume this can grow without bound and overload the API server and legacy backend. Use a bounded worker pool/queue with defined overload behavior.

Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response

The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the REST handler returns, that parent context is normally cancelled, which immediately cancels the child context and can prevent the legacy Create from reaching storage. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. This makes replication scheduler-dependent and can leave legacy permanently stale even though the unified write was reported successful. Create an independent background context (while preserving required request values such as tenant identity) and track/drain it as part of shutdown.

The new mode-3 integration test assumes legacy replication is synchronous

The mode-3 subtest invokes doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares legacy API results after Kubernetes creates, updates, and deletes (for example the legacy list at line 522 and the legacy reads in getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 intentionally performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so these assertions race the replica goroutines and will be flaky with a slow legacy backend. Wait eventually for the expected legacy state, or expose a test hook to drain the replica queue before asserting it.

Unit tests do not verify the asynchronous replica calls

The tests return immediately after the primary operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, ls and us wrap the same mock instance (lines 53-54), so an unconstrained expectation set up for Storage can also satisfy Legacy; no AssertExpectations call checks either call count or destination. Consequently these tests can pass if replication is delayed, omitted, or sent to the wrong store. Use separate mocks and a channel/WaitGroup or a deterministic replica executor to assert legacy execution, error handling, and timeout behavior.

Update replays the update transform against a different store state

The legacy Update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has already consumed it. UpdatedObjectInfo produces an object from the current old object, so patches, applies, resource-version checks, and stateful transformers can produce a different result when invoked again against the legacy object's state. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated and wrapped the update before writing both stores; removing that behavior means mode 3 can report a successful unified update while applying different content, or a conflict, in legacy. Preserve a prepared update/result and the necessary resource-version translation when issuing the asynchronous replica write.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recheck the cache after acquiring the writer lock

A caller that observes a nil cache on the read path unconditionally reloads the manifest after it eventually acquires the writer lock. If several callers observe nil before the first caller obtains that lock, they will each parse the manifest serially and overwrite an already populated cache. A burst of initial requests can therefore be delayed by N serialized disk reads rather than sharing the first initialization. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` under the write lock for non-development requests before loading the manifest; development mode can retain its intentional reload behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
The error message and retained feature-toggle documentation misstate the feature status

SQL expressions are now deliberately disabled regardless of the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle, but this reports only that they are "not implemented." Operators who have enabled the documented toggle will receive a misleading error and have no indication that their configuration is intentionally ignored due to the security removal. Update the user-facing error and feature-toggle documentation to state that SQL expressions are disabled/removed and, where appropriate, reference the security advisory.

The permanent SQL-expression disablement has no regression coverage

This PR changes no test files, so there is no test that verifies a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled. That is the primary security boundary here: `enableSqlExpressions` intentionally returns false in both toggle states. Add coverage for the enabled-toggle case (and the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path, which is disabled through the stub DB) so a future cleanup cannot inadvertently re-enable the RCE/LFI-prone implementation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing a backend watch channel can panic the server during shutdown

This receive does not check the channel's ok result before dereferencing v. A normal backend shutdown closes its event channel (the SQL poller closes its stream), after which this loop receives a nil *WrittenEvent and panics while evaluating v.Type. Stop invokes Lifecycle.Stop before s.cancel, and this PR now starts initWatcher during every ResourceServer construction, so even servers that never serve a request can hit this shutdown crash. Exit the loop when the channel is closed and make the loop observe cancellation.

Failed eager initialization leaves partially started resources running

If search.init succeeds and starts its watch goroutine but initWatcher subsequently fails, NewResourceServer returns an error without calling cancel or Lifecycle.Stop. No ResourceServer is returned to the caller, so it cannot later be stopped; the search watcher is particularly leaked because it was created with context.Background(). Ensure constructor failure cleans up the server context and any successfully initialized lifecycle resources before returning the error.

Parallel index workers race on totalBatchesIndexed

errgroup runs these functions concurrently when WorkerThreads is greater than one, but each one increments the shared totalBatchesIndexed integer without synchronization. This is a Go data race, causes race-detector failures, and can emit an incorrect tracing count. Use an atomic counter or collect per-worker results after the group completes.

Startup index build drops writes committed while indexes are being built

The indexes are populated from ListIterator snapshots before the write-event watch is opened. The SQL WatchWriteEvents implementation initializes its cursor from the latest resource versions at subscription time, so any write committed after an index's list snapshot but before this call is treated as already seen and is never sent to handleEvent. In HA deployments, writes from another server during startup can therefore leave added documents missing, modified documents stale, or deleted documents searchable until another relevant write occurs. Start/buffer the watch before building, or replay events from the resource version returned by each build.

The eagerly started search watcher panics when its event stream closes

The search watcher also receives from events without checking whether the channel was closed. On normal SQL backend shutdown the poller closes the stream, causing v to be nil and handleEvent to dereference it. This is now started during construction whenever search is configured, and it uses context.Background(), so server cancellation does not stop it. Check the receive ok value and use a server-owned cancellable context for the watcher.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New test cleanup registrations remove a nonexistent literal alias

Each provider created in the loop registers cleanup for `identityProviders().get("alias")` rather than for the generated `idp-alias-<n>` alias; the same mistake is repeated for `idp-alias-20` at line 425. The cleanup therefore does not remove the providers created by this test, which can leave test data behind and contaminate subsequent tests or cause cleanup failures. Register cleanup using the actual alias for each created representation.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384 and ES512 tests do not use their required elliptic curves

Thus the ES384 and ES512 cases sign with P-256 coordinates padded to the requested output length, rather than exercising P-384 and P-521 coordinate sizes and DER edge cases. The test also only checks conversion round-tripping, not whether the reconstructed signature verifies. Equal provider priorities make FIPS selection depend on classpath order

The built-in Default, Elytron, and FIPS providers all return priority 200. For providers with the same priority, this sort preserves the ServiceLoader encounter order, which is determined by classpath/resource order rather than an explicit security policy. Consequently, when both the default and FIPS service descriptors are visible, the default provider can be selected and the FIPS provider merely logged as ignored; previously this unsafe combination failed fast. Give the intended FIPS provider a distinct higher priority or reject ties for the highest priority.

The selected authz crypto provider cannot perform documented JWT client authentication

`AuthzClient.create` initializes this provider in a standalone authz-client runtime, but this implementation throws `UnsupportedOperationException` for both PEM handling here and JWS signature creation in `getSignature` (line 219). The authz client documents JWT client credentials as a supported credential type; that flow must parse the configured private key and sign a client assertion, so it will fail once this provider is selected. Provide the standard JCA/PEM implementations for these operations, or avoid installing this incomplete provider as the global CryptoIntegration provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client deletion skips V2 permission-resource cleanup

The removal listener is now gated by `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`, but V2 authorization is selected using the distinct `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` feature. true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

Startup index build drops writes committed while indexes are being built

The indexes are populated from ListIterator snapshots before the write-event watch is opened. The SQL WatchWriteEvents implementation initializes its cursor from the latest resource versions at subscription time, so any write committed after an index's list snapshot but before this call is treated as already seen and is never sent to handleEvent. Closing a backend watch channel can panic the server during shutdown

The eagerly started search watcher panics when its event stream closes

false_positives.candidate:
Use of Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs breaks supported runtimes

`queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged here), leaving workers blocked forever in `get()`. Each subsequent `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` then waits the full timeout, so the default 20 queues can make every consumer shutdown take roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon workers. An exception raised while processing work also attempts to resolve `queue.ShutDown` in the exception handler and can terminate the worker with an `AttributeError`. Use a compatible sentinel/event-based shutdown mechanism or require and enforce Python 3.13.

Closing one assignment permanently disables the factory-owned pool

The pool is created once on `ResultsStrategyFactory` and is shared by every strategy returned from `create_with_partitions`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` shuts that shared pool down. After a Kafka partition revoke/reassignment causes Arroyo to close/terminate one strategy and create another from the same factory, the new strategy receives the already-shut-down pool and no workers. On Python 3.13, `Queue.put()` then raises `ShutDown`, and `submit()` catches that error and marks the offset complete, so the new strategy can commit messages that were never processed. On older Python versions, the puts succeed into queues with no workers and offsets never advance. The pool must be scoped to a single strategy assignment or recreated/reset after strategy teardown.

The worker queues are unbounded, so the new mode provides no backpressure

`queue.Queue()` defaults to `maxsize=0`, meaning `FixedQueuePool.submit()` never blocks regardless of how far a slow worker falls behind. The consumer will continue decoding and retaining every fetched message (including both the decoded result and original `Message`) in memory while lag grows. A slow remote-subscription handler can therefore cause unbounded memory growth and OOM the consumer, contrary to the strategy's stated backpressure guarantee. Configure a bounded queue size and integrate blocking/full-queue handling with the consumer's polling/backpressure behavior.

The purported graceful shutdown abandons queued work before a final commit

Workers are marked `shutdown=True` before their queues are shut down. A worker that is currently processing exits after that item, and a worker that was blocked in `get()` processes at most one item before its next loop-condition check exits; remaining queued items are never drained. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` also stops and joins the commit thread before this worker shutdown, so an item finishing during shutdown has no later commit opportunity. This causes arbitrary accepted work to be replayed after normal deploys/rebalances, potentially duplicating side effects and creating large restart backlogs. Shutdown should drain accepted work (or deliberately cancel it with a coordinated retry policy) and commit completed offsets after the drain.

false_positives.candidate:
The Redis value type change is not compatible with existing live buffers

Existing `span-buf:s:*` keys are Redis SETs written by the previous version, while this version issues `ZADD` against the same keys. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for that operation (and the new Lua script's `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` calls also fail on those keys). During a rolling deployment, any active segment from the preceding version will make span processing fail rather than commit its Kafka batch, and old workers will likewise fail if they encounter a newly-created sorted set. Use versioned keys or an explicit migration/rollout strategy before changing the Redis datatype.

ZUNIONSTORE changes span timestamps when buffers overlap

`ZUNIONSTORE` uses `SUM` as its default score aggregation. If a payload already exists in both the destination buffer and a buffer being merged—for example, when an at-least-once replay overlaps a previously buffered descendant—the resulting score becomes twice its `end_timestamp_precise` value. The score is now used to choose entries for `ZPOPMIN`, so these duplicated members look artificially newer and cause the wrong spans to be retained or evicted. Merge with an aggregation that preserves the timestamp (such as `MAX`) rather than the default sum.

Insertion eviction ignores the configured segment span limit

`SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` remains a constructor setting, but the prior enforcement of that setting was removed from `_load_segment_data` and no limit is passed into this Lua script. The script instead always retains exactly 1000 members. Deployments configured with any other limit now silently discard spans at 1000 (and the default behavior changes from allowing 1001 members to retaining 1000), so the buffer configuration no longer controls its documented capacity.

Reducing redirect traversal fragments deep out-of-order traces

The redirect traversal bound was reduced from 10,000 to 1,000 without handling the case where the bound is reached. A valid deeply nested trace ingested from child toward root can create a redirect chain longer than 1,000 entries; subsequent spans then stop at an intermediate buffer and are mapped there instead of to the true segment root. This splits one trace into separately flushed segments and assigns incorrect segment IDs.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response

The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the REST handler returns, that parent context is normally cancelled, which immediately cancels the child context and can prevent the legacy Create from reaching storage. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. This makes replication scheduler-dependent and can leave legacy permanently stale even though the unified write was reported successful. Create an independent background context (while preserving required request values such as tenant identity) and track/drain it as part of shutdown.

Asynchronous replica writes can be applied out of order

Each successful primary write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a unified Create followed by a unified Delete can schedule a slow legacy Create and a fast legacy Delete; the delete runs first against an absent legacy object, then the delayed create leaves the object present in legacy after it is deleted in unified storage. Since mode 3 reads unified storage, this divergence is hidden until a legacy endpoint is used or a rollback occurs. Replica writes need a serialized queue or per-key ordering mechanism.

Every write creates an unbounded 10-second background operation

There is no queue, semaphore, or worker limit around the goroutine per write. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, each incoming write can retain a goroutine, request data, and a legacy connection attempt for up to ten seconds. At normal write volume this can grow without bound and overload the API server and legacy backend. Use a bounded worker pool/queue with defined overload behavior.

Update replays the update transform against a different store state

The legacy Update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has already consumed it. UpdatedObjectInfo produces an object from the current old object, so patches, applies, resource-version checks, and stateful transformers can produce a different result when invoked again against the legacy object's state. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated and wrapped the update before writing both stores; removing that behavior means mode 3 can report a successful unified update while applying different content, or a conflict, in legacy. Preserve a prepared update/result and the necessary resource-version translation when issuing the asynchronous replica write.

A primary NotFound no longer cleans up a stale legacy object

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error. The prior implementation treated a unified-storage NotFound specially: it still issued Legacy.Delete while returning the primary NotFound result. If the stores have already drifted, deleting an object that is absent in unified storage now leaves the stale legacy object intact and still available through legacy paths (or after rollback). Retain the legacy cleanup attempt for primary NotFound errors.

Several mode-3 duration measurements are recorded against the wrong store

When Storage.Create fails, this records a legacy duration rather than a storage duration; Update has the same error at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 records a storage duration. This hides primary failures and reports legacy failures as storage failures, so dashboards and alerts cannot accurately detect replication or unified-storage health. Record each operation on its corresponding collector.

Unit tests do not verify the asynchronous replica calls

The tests return immediately after the primary operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, ls and us wrap the same mock instance (lines 53-54), so an unconstrained expectation set up for Storage can also satisfy Legacy; no AssertExpectations call checks either call count or destination. Consequently these tests can pass if replication is delayed, omitted, or sent to the wrong store. Use separate mocks and a channel/WaitGroup or a deterministic replica executor to assert legacy execution, error handling, and timeout behavior.

The new mode-3 integration test assumes legacy replication is synchronous

The mode-3 subtest invokes doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares legacy API results after Kubernetes creates, updates, and deletes (for example the legacy list at line 522 and the legacy reads in getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 intentionally performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so these assertions race the replica goroutines and will be flaky with a slow legacy backend. Wait eventually for the expected legacy state, or expose a test hook to drain the replica queue before asserting it.

The validator calls the mutating `BlockedEmail.should_block?` every time validations run. `UsersController#create` first calls `user.valid?` before the Discourse Hub check and then calls `user.save`, which validates again even when the first validation failed. Consequently one blocked registration request increments `match_count` twice and records two matches, so the statistics no longer represent blocked signup attempts. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same root cause: the read/predicate method (`should_block?` / `should_block_email?`) has side effects by updating match statistics. The candidate issue further explains a concrete bug resulting from this anti-pattern (double counting during validations), which directly aligns with the golden comment's concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows attackers to bypass email blocks simply by changing the casing of the email address.

false_positives.candidate:

The counter is updated through a read-modify-write sequence on an ordinary Active Record instance. Concurrent validations of the same blocked address can both read the same `match_count` and save the same incremented value, losing matches; a delayed save can also overwrite a newer `last_match_at` with an older timestamp. After the server rejects a blocked email, the UI can retain its previous successful validation and re-enable submission instead of showing the email as invalid. The previous `float: right` was removed, so in those browsers `.panel` is placed directly after the title/extra information instead of at the right side of the header, breaking the navigation layout. true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Serializer attribute predicates in this class use the `include_<attribute>?` form (for example `include_email?`). `include_website_name` lacks the question mark, so the serializer will not use it to decide whether to emit the attribute. Consequently `website_name` is emitted by default even for profiles without a website or with an unparsable URL, producing an unintended `null` field rather than being omitted as this method attempts to specify. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main problem in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix for Rails serializer conditional inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the primary bug is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:

As a result, those responses now expose the host portion of a profile website (for example an employer or personal site) despite the website field being intentionally hidden. true_positives.matched_candidate:

`contents` is appended directly to a footer that interpolates `url` into an HTML attribute, then the post is created with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` returns raw HTML unchanged and the embed view renders `post.cooked` with `raw`. `PollFeed` supplies HTML-decoded feed content, so a feed item containing `<script>` or event attributes becomes stored XSS on the Discourse origin. true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues: a NoMethodError when `contents` is nil, and an XSS vulnerability from unescaped `url` interpolation in the generated HTML. The candidate issue directly identifies the XSS vulnerability caused by interpolating `url` into the single-quoted `href` attribute without escaping (as well as unsanitized `contents`). true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`<%- end if %>` emits the Ruby tokens `end if` with no condition, which is invalid Ruby syntax. The template is compiled when an existing embedded topic is rendered, so after retrieval succeeds requests to `embed/best` will fail with a template syntax error instead of displaying the discussion. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `end if` instead of `end` in an ERB template, resulting in invalid Ruby syntax at render/compile time.

false_positives.candidate:
Remote import follows redirects outside the validated host

The host check in `TopicRetriever` validates only the originally supplied URL, but `open(url).read` follows HTTP redirects and no subsequent destination is checked. A requester can select a path on the configured embeddable host; if that host has an open redirect, the Discourse server can be induced to fetch an arbitrary internal URL such as a cloud metadata endpoint. The Referer check does not prevent direct clients from sending a forged Referer header. Disable redirects or validate every redirect target's scheme, host, port, and resolved IP range before fetching.

Embed creation is not atomic despite the unique URL index

The code reads the embed row and only later creates it, with no lock or unique-conflict recovery. Concurrent feed polls/retrieval jobs can both observe no row and both create a topic; the loser then raises on the unique `embed_url` index. The outer transaction rolls back that loser, but `PostCreator` has already published MessageBus events and enqueued post-processing work before this transaction commits, leaving failed jobs/phantom notifications. Use an atomic create-or-find strategy (or rescue the unique violation and reload), and avoid publishing work until the outer transaction has committed.

Each new embed request can trigger a complete feed import

For every missing embed URL, retrieval synchronously invokes `PollFeed`, which downloads and parses the entire configured feed and iterates every item before attempting the requested page. The Redis throttle is keyed by the full embed URL, so requests with distinct query strings bypass one another, and the public endpoint can queue those jobs with a forged Referer header. With feed polling enabled this permits unbounded feed downloads and import passes, exhausting workers and potentially overloading the feed source. Use a global feed-poll lock/cache (the existing `feed_key` is unused) and leave full polling to the scheduled job.

Feed polling uses a String method unavailable on supported Ruby versions

`String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1. This application still supports the Rails 3/4-era Ruby versions through its dual-boot Gemfile, including Ruby 1.9/2.0, where this line raises `NoMethodError` for every feed item and makes feed polling unusable. Use an encoding cleanup compatible with the supported Ruby versions or explicitly raise the minimum Ruby version.

On the PostgreSQL versions contemporary with this application, adding a column with both a non-null default and `null: false` rewrites the entire `posts` table while holding a strong table lock. On a production forum this can block reads/writes for the duration of a large table rewrite during deployment. Add the column without a default/not-null constraint, backfill in batches, then set the default and constraint in later migrations.

Non-root-relative links and images resolve against the Discourse embed URL

`absolutize_urls` only rewrites values beginning with `/`. Common source markup such as `href="article.html"`, `href="../article"`, or `src="images/photo.jpg"` remains relative; when rendered inside the Discourse iframe, browsers resolve those URLs relative to `/embed/best` on the Discourse host rather than the imported article. This breaks links and assets for many imported pages. Resolve all relative href/src values against the source URL (for example with `URI.join`) while leaving already absolute URLs unchanged.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

`validateUploadedFile` receives the upload type, but this change replaces both `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` with a fixed 10 MB limit. ImageMagick is invoked on unbounded direct uploads before server-side validation

The resize loop runs before `Upload.create_for` performs the normal upload validation at line 72, and there is no server-side maximum for the original multipart file before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`. The option passed here is `allow_animated_thumbnails`, but this operation rewrites the original uploaded file rather than a thumbnail. true_positives.matched_candidate:
The endpoint crashes for users without an existing TopicUser row

`find_by` can return nil for a logged-in user who has never visited or otherwise interacted with the topic, which is normal for a public topic reachable through this route. The following `tu.notification_level` dereference then raises a NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of applying the requested preference. false_positives.candidate:
The unsubscribe action changes preferences through a CSRF-able GET request

This GET endpoint directly changes and saves the current user's notification preference, while it is explicitly allowed outside the normal XHR path and has no signed recipient token or confirmation step. Topic URLs are predictable for public topics, so a third-party site can force an authenticated visitor to navigate to one and mute/downgrade that visitor's topic notifications; browser prefetchers or link scanners can also trigger the change. The GET should only render a confirmation, with the mutation performed by a CSRF-protected POST, or the email link should use a recipient-bound signed token with appropriate one-click semantics.

Directly saving TopicUser bypasses notification preference invariants

This save bypasses `TopicUser.change`, the standard path that sets `notifications_changed_at`, records `notifications_reason_id` as `user_changed`, and publishes the level change. In particular, topic-user records created only while sending an email have a nil notification reason; after this action leaves that reason nil, the auto-track logic in `TopicUser.update_last_read` is allowed to promote a muted user back to tracking when they later read the topic. Other open clients also do not receive the MessageBus update. Compute the desired level and persist it through `TopicUser.change` so the unsubscribe is recorded as an explicit user choice.

The added test does not verify that the per-topic unsubscribe URL is rendered

The test now supplies `unsubscribe_url`, but its only body assertion checks for the unchanged user-preferences URL. It never asserts that `/t/1234/unsubscribe` appears in the text or HTML email, so the suite would still pass if the new interpolation were omitted or the per-topic link were broken. false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting the cache does not refresh the cache-status query

The delete mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query supplying `cacheUpdatedAt`. Consumers that do not provide an `onChanged` callback that explicitly refetches will continue to show the old "Last updated" value and delete action after the server has deleted the rows; this is especially persistent because the query disables refetch-on-window-focus. Invalidate or refetch `connectedCalendars` when the deletion settles.

Adding this required column with `DEFAULT NOW()` gives every pre-existing CalendarCache row the time the migration runs. The new status query takes the maximum of this field and the UI presents it as "Last updated", so existing cache data will be reported as freshly updated at deployment even if it was fetched much earlier. This bypasses the repository lockfile and makes `dev:cron` nondeterministic. Add and pin `tsx` as a development dependency and invoke it through Yarn/the package binary.

`cleanup` always exits with status 0, but it is also called when Tunnelmole is rate-limited or no tunnel URL can be extracted. As a result, an automated setup/test invocation reports success even though `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` was not configured and subsequent webhook testing cannot work. Preserve a nonzero exit code for error paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

Working-hours validation ignores the booking duration

Both start and end are calculated from slotStartTime, so the condition only checks whether the slot starts within a fixed host's working hours. A one-hour slot beginning at 11:30 for a host working until 12:00 passes this check even though it ends at 12:30. Although getTimeSlots normally constrains the host that generated a candidate, a loose round-robin host can generate this candidate and this new fixed-host filter is then responsible for rejecting it. Calculate end from slotEndTime and require the complete slot to fit.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: that `end` is erroneously calculated using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Equal override endpoints are compared by object identity

Each dayjs(...).add(...) call creates a distinct Dayjs object, so strict equality is always false even when date.start and date.end represent the same instant. The special handling for a zero-length/all-day-unavailable override therefore never runs. A candidate that starts exactly at that instant can fall through to dateOverrideExist and be considered available; compare the timestamps with isSame() instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: comparing two `dayjs(...).add(...)` objects using strict equality (`===`), which compares object references rather than timestamps and always evaluates to false. Both recommend using `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours validation treats no matching interval as available

The predicate searches for any working-hours interval that the slot is outside of, rather than requiring an interval that contains the slot. If a fixed host has no working-hours row on that weekday, find() returns undefined and the host is treated as available. It also rejects every slot for a host with split hours: a 10:00 slot in a 09:00-12:00 interval is rejected because it is outside the separate 13:00-17:00 interval. In a round-robin event, slots generated by a loose host can therefore be offered while a fixed host is unavailable, or valid fixed-host slots can all disappear. This should use a positive containment check over the host's intervals.

Override timezone conversion is adjusted a second time across DST

The override minutes are already translated using the organizer and invitee offsets at the override timestamp, but buildSlots subsequently adds organizerDSTDiff - inviteeDSTDiff based on the current date and the invitee day. This shifts date overrides by an hour whenever the override date has a different DST offset than today. For example, when evaluated in January, a 10:00 America/New_York override in July for a UTC invitee is converted here to 14:00, then buildSlots applies the -60 minute organizer DST difference and produces 13:00. Date overrides are dated absolute exceptions and must not receive the recurring-working-hours DST correction again.

The claimed fixed-host round-robin behavior has no regression coverage

The added timezone assertion exercises a regular one-user event only. It does not create a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host, a loose host whose availability generates the candidate slot, and a fixed-host date override. The existing round-robin test also has no fixed hosts. Consequently the new fixed-host filtering path, including the case this PR is intended to prevent, is untested and the overbooking and split-availability regressions can merge unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count updates can lose concurrent failures

In the recurring/all-remaining path, each updated booking's calendar reference is obtained with `.find(...)`, so only its first calendar event is considered. The code then tries that one reference with every credential belonging to the booking owner, rather than using the credential attached to each reference. With multiple collective-host references, secondary host events are never deleted, and the first event is redundantly deleted once per reference (often using credentials that cannot access it). The only changed end-to-end assertion adjusts a webhook payload shape; it does not create a collective event with two hosts, distinct credentials, and distinct destination calendars. This causes arbitrary accepted work to be replayed after normal deploys/rebalances, potentially duplicating side effects and creating large restart backlogs. Raw substring matching applies upsampling to non-error Discover queries

The Discover eligibility check treats any query containing the text `event.type:error` as error-only. Valid queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, `!event.type:error`, or a quoted search term containing that text therefore have `count()` replaced with `upsampled_count()`. The new test uses a Go 1.21 builtin while the repository targets Go 1.20

Several mode-3 duration measurements are recorded against the wrong store

Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 records a storage duration. This hides primary failures and reports legacy failures as storage failures, so dashboards and alerts cannot accurately detect replication or unified-storage health. It describes the swap as the reverse of the golden (legacy call recording storage duration). true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Successful delete metrics use an object name as the resource label

The third argument to recordStorageDuration is the resource/kind label; every other mode-3 path passes options.Kind. This successful-delete path passes name instead, creating a distinct Prometheus time series for every deleted object and making success and failure metrics use incompatible labels. true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the same problem: the delete path's metrics recording passes name where the other methods pass options.Kind. The candidate goes further and spells out the cardinality impact.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response

The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the REST handler returns, that parent context is normally cancelled, which immediately cancels the child context and can prevent the legacy Create from reaching storage. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. This makes replication scheduler-dependent and can leave legacy permanently stale even though the unified write was reported successful. Create an independent background context (while preserving required request values such as tenant identity) and track/drain it as part of shutdown.

Asynchronous replica writes can be applied out of order

Each successful primary write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a unified Create followed by a unified Delete can schedule a slow legacy Create and a fast legacy Delete; the delete runs first against an absent legacy object, then the delayed create leaves the object present in legacy after it is deleted in unified storage. Since mode 3 reads unified storage, this divergence is hidden until a legacy endpoint is used or a rollback occurs. Replica writes need a serialized queue or per-key ordering mechanism.

Every write creates an unbounded 10-second background operation

There is no queue, semaphore, or worker limit around the goroutine per write. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, each incoming write can retain a goroutine, request data, and a legacy connection attempt for up to ten seconds. At normal write volume this can grow without bound and overload the API server and legacy backend. Use a bounded worker pool/queue with defined overload behavior.

Update replays the update transform against a different store state

The legacy Update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has already consumed it. UpdatedObjectInfo produces an object from the current old object, so patches, applies, resource-version checks, and stateful transformers can produce a different result when invoked again against the legacy object's state. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated and wrapped the update before writing both stores; removing that behavior means mode 3 can report a successful unified update while applying different content, or a conflict, in legacy. Preserve a prepared update/result and the necessary resource-version translation when issuing the asynchronous replica write.

A primary NotFound no longer cleans up a stale legacy object

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error. The prior implementation treated a unified-storage NotFound specially: it still issued Legacy.Delete while returning the primary NotFound result. If the stores have already drifted, deleting an object that is absent in unified storage now leaves the stale legacy object intact and still available through legacy paths (or after rollback). Retain the legacy cleanup attempt for primary NotFound errors.

Unit tests do not verify the asynchronous replica calls

The tests return immediately after the primary operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, ls and us wrap the same mock instance (lines 53-54), so an unconstrained expectation set up for Storage can also satisfy Legacy; no AssertExpectations call checks either call count or destination. Consequently these tests can pass if replication is delayed, omitted, or sent to the wrong store. Use separate mocks and a channel/WaitGroup or a deterministic replica executor to assert legacy execution, error handling, and timeout behavior.

The new mode-3 integration test assumes legacy replication is synchronous

The mode-3 subtest invokes doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares legacy API results after Kubernetes creates, updates, and deletes (for example the legacy list at line 522 and the legacy reads in getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 intentionally performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so these assertions race the replica goroutines and will be flaky with a slow legacy backend. Wait eventually for the expected legacy state, or expose a test hook to drain the replica queue before asserting it.

`String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1. false_positives.candidate:
Use of Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs breaks supported runtimes

`queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier supported Python versions, `q.shutdown(...)` raises `AttributeError` (which is only logged here), leaving workers blocked forever in `get()`. Each subsequent `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` then waits the full timeout, so the default 20 queues can make every consumer shutdown take roughly 100 seconds and leak daemon workers. An exception raised while processing work also attempts to resolve `queue.ShutDown` in the exception handler and can terminate the worker with an `AttributeError`. Use a compatible sentinel/event-based shutdown mechanism or require and enforce Python 3.13.

Closing one assignment permanently disables the factory-owned pool

The pool is created once on `ResultsStrategyFactory` and is shared by every strategy returned from `create_with_partitions`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` shuts that shared pool down. After a Kafka partition revoke/reassignment causes Arroyo to close/terminate one strategy and create another from the same factory, the new strategy receives the already-shut-down pool and no workers. On Python 3.13, `Queue.put()` then raises `ShutDown`, and `submit()` catches that error and marks the offset complete, so the new strategy can commit messages that were never processed. On older Python versions, the puts succeed into queues with no workers and offsets never advance. The pool must be scoped to a single strategy assignment or recreated/reset after strategy teardown.

The worker queues are unbounded, so the new mode provides no backpressure

`queue.Queue()` defaults to `maxsize=0`, meaning `FixedQueuePool.submit()` never blocks regardless of how far a slow worker falls behind. The consumer will continue decoding and retaining every fetched message (including both the decoded result and original `Message`) in memory while lag grows. A slow remote-subscription handler can therefore cause unbounded memory growth and OOM the consumer, contrary to the strategy's stated backpressure guarantee. Configure a bounded queue size and integrate blocking/full-queue handling with the consumer's polling/backpressure behavior.

The purported graceful shutdown abandons queued work before a final commit

Workers are marked `shutdown=True` before their queues are shut down. A worker that is currently processing exits after that item, and a worker that was blocked in `get()` processes at most one item before its next loop-condition check exits; remaining queued items are never drained. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` also stops and joins the commit thread before this worker shutdown, so an item finishing during shutdown has no later commit opportunity. This causes arbitrary accepted work to be replayed after normal deploys/rebalances, potentially duplicating side effects and creating large restart backlogs. Shutdown should drain accepted work (or deliberately cancel it with a coordinated retry policy) and commit completed offsets after the drain.
